Hypergeometric functions and hyperbolic metric

G. D. Anderson, T. Sugawa, M. K. Vamanamurthy, and M. Vuorinen
Abstract.

We obtain new inequalities for certain hypergeometric functions. Using these inequalities, we deduce estimates for the hyperbolic metric and the induced distance function on a certain canonical hyperbolic plane domain.

Key words and phrases: 
Hypergeometric functions, complete elliptic integrals, convexity, Poincaré density
2000 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary 30F45, Secondary 33C05, 33C75, 33E05.

1. Introduction

The hyperbolic metric is one of the most important tools for the study of properties of analytic functions. A plane domain Ω\Omega is called hyperbolic if it admits a complete Riemannian metric of constant curvature −4.-4. The metric is called the hyperbolic metric of Ω\Omega and denoted by ρΩ​(z).\rho_{\Omega}(z). We denote by dΩ​(z,w)d_{\Omega}(z,w) the hyperbolic distance on Ω,\Omega, which is induced by ρΩ.\rho_{\Omega}. It is well known that a domain in the complex plane ℂ\mathbb{C} is hyperbolic if and only if the boundary contains at least two points. For instance, the unit disk 𝔻={z∈ℂ:|z|<1}\mathbb{D}=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|<1\} has ρ𝔻​(z)=1/(1−|z|2)\rho_{\mathbb{D}}(z)=1/(1-|z|^{2}) and d𝔻​(z,w)=arctanh⁡(|z−w|/|1−w¯​z|).d_{\mathbb{D}}(z,w)={\operatorname{arctanh}\,}(|z-w|/|1-\bar{w}z|).

We recall the principle of hyperbolic metric, which is very useful in the study of conformal invariants [Ah]. Let DD and Ω\Omega be hyperbolic domains. For an analytic map f:D→Ω,f:D\to\Omega, this principle implies that the inequality ρΩ​(f⁡(z))​|f′​(z)|≤ρD​(z)\rho_{\Omega}(f(z))|f^{\prime}(z)|\leq\rho_{D}(z) holds, implying that dΩ​(f⁡(z),f⁡(w))≤dD​(z,w)d_{\Omega}(f(z),f(w))\leq d_{D}(z,w) for z,w∈D.z,w\in D. Thus, a lower estimate for dΩ​(w0,w)d_{\Omega}(w_{0},w) in terms of |w||w| (for a fixed w0w_{0}) will lead to a growth estimate for an analytic function f:D→Ωf:D\to\Omega with f⁡(z0)=w0f(z_{0})=w_{0} for a fixed z0∈D.z_{0}\in D. Similarly, a lower estimate for ρΩ\rho_{\Omega} yields a distortion theorem for an analytic function on DD taking values in Ω.\Omega.

Since the twice-punctured plane ℂ∖{a,b}\mathbb{C}\setminus\{a,b\} is a maximal hyperbolic domain, it is of particular importance. We write λa,b=ρℂ∖{a,b}\lambda_{a,b}=\rho_{\mathbb{C}\setminus\{a,b\}} and da,b=dℂ∖{a,b}d_{a,b}=d_{\mathbb{C}\setminus\{a,b\}} for short. Noting the obvious relations

λ0,1​(z)=|b−a|​λa,b​((b−a)​z+a),d0,1​(z,w)=da,b​((b−a)​z+a,(b−a)​w+a),\lambda_{0,1}(z)=|b-a|\lambda_{a,b}((b-a)z+a),\quad d_{0,1}(z,w)=d_{a,b}((b-a)z+a,(b-a)w+a),

we may restrict our attention to the case when a=0a=0 and b=1.b=1. Precise information about λ0,1​(z)\lambda_{0,1}(z) and d0,1​(z,w)d_{0,1}(z,w) leads to sharp forms of classical results in function theory such as the Landau, Schottky, and Picard theorems (cf. [Ah], [H1], [H2]) as well as various useful estimates for the hyperbolic metric of a general plane domain (cf. [BP], [SV]).

Since the inequalities

λ0,1​(−|z|)≤λ0,1​(z)andd0,1​(−|z|,−|w|)≤d0,1​(z,w)\lambda_{0,1}(-|z|)\leq\lambda_{0,1}(z)\quad\text{and}\quad d_{0,1}(-|z|,-|w|)\leq d_{0,1}(z,w)

hold for z,w∈ℂ∖{0,1}z,w\in\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0,1\} (see [LVV]), lower estimates for λ0,1\lambda_{0,1} and d0,1d_{0,1} reduce to the analysis of these quantities on the negative real axis.

It is known (cf. [SV]) that λ0,1​(−x)\lambda_{0,1}(-x) and d0,1​(−x,−y)d_{0,1}(-x,-y) can be expressed in terms of complete elliptic integrals of the first kind for x,y>0x,y>0:

λ0,1​(−x)\displaystyle\lambda_{0,1}(-x) =π8​x​𝒦​(r)​𝒦​(r′),and\displaystyle=\frac{\pi}{8x{\mathcal{K}}(r){\mathcal{K}}(r^{\prime})},\quad\text{and}
d0,1​(−x,−y)\displaystyle d_{0,1}(-x,-y) =|Φ⁡(x)−Φ⁡(y)|,\displaystyle=|\Phi(x)-\Phi(y)|,

where

(1.1) Φ⁡(x)\displaystyle\Phi(x) =12​log⁡𝒦⁡(r)𝒦⁡(r′),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\log\frac{{\mathcal{K}}(r)}{{\mathcal{K}}(r^{\prime})},
r=x1+x,r′\displaystyle r=\sqrt{\frac{x}{1+x}},\quad r^{\prime} =1−r2=11+x,\displaystyle=\sqrt{1-r^{2}}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{1+x}},

and

𝒦⁡(r)=∫01d​t(1−t2)​(1−r2​t2){\mathcal{K}}(r)=\int_{0}^{1}\frac{dt}{\sqrt{(1-t^{2})(1-r^{2}t^{2})}}

is the complete elliptic integral of the first kind. Note that the function Φ\Phi satisfies the relation Φ⁡(1/x)=−Φ⁡(x)\Phi(1/x)=-\Phi(x) for x>0.x>0. In particular, Φ⁡(1)=0\Phi(1)=0 and hence Φ⁡(x)=d0,1​(−x,−1)\Phi(x)=d_{0,1}(-x,-1) for x≥1.x\geq 1. Note also that Φ\Phi can be expressed by 2​Φ​(x)=−log⁡(2​μ​(r)/π),2\Phi(x)=-\log(2\mu(r)/\pi), where μ⁡(r)\mu(r) denotes the well-known modulus of the Grötzsch ring 𝔻∖[0,r]\mathbb{D}\setminus[0,r] given by μ⁡(r)=(π/2)​𝒦​(r′)/𝒦⁡(r)\mu(r)=(\pi/2)\mathcal{K}(r^{\prime})/\mathcal{K}(r), for r∈(0,1)r\in(0,1), and where 𝔻\mathbb{D} is the unit disk {z:|z|<1}\{z:|z|<1\} in the complex plane ℂ\mathbb{C} (see [LV] or [AVV1] for details).

Since

(1.2) 𝒦⁡(r)=π2​F​(12,12,1,r2){\mathcal{K}}(r)=\frac{\pi}{2}F\left(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2};1;r^{2}\right)

in terms of the Gaussian hypergeometric function with specific parameters (cf. [AVV1, (3.13)]), inequalities for hypergeometric functions will lead to estimates for the hyperbolic metric.

In the present paper, we give several inequalities for hypergeometric functions with restricted parameters. By using these inequalities, we deduce estimates for the hyperbolic metric and hyperbolic distance of the twice-punctured plane ℂ∖{0,1}.\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0,1\}. In particular, we prove some of the conjectures proposed in [SV]. Inequalities for hypergeometric functions have applications also in the study of the hyperbolic metric with conical singularities as in [ASVV].

2. Preliminaries

In this section, we recall some definitions and properties of special functions [R], and state two results that are particularly useful in proving monotonicity of a quotient of two functions [AVV1],[HVV].

Given complex numbers aa, bb, and cc with c≠0,−1,−2,…,c\neq 0,-1,-2,\dots, the Gaussian hypergeometric function is defined as

(2.1) F⁡(a,b,c,z)=F12​(a,b,c,z)≡∑n=0∞(a,n)​(b,n)(c,n)​znn!,|z|<1,F(a,b;c;z)\!=\!{}_{2}F_{1}(a,b;c;z)\!\equiv\!\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(a,n)(b,n)}{(c,n)}\frac{z^{n}}{n!},\quad|z|<1,

and then is continued analytically to the slit plane ℂ∖[1,∞)\mathbb{C}\setminus[1,\infty). Here (a,n)(a,n) is the shifted factorial function, namely, (a,0)=1(a,0)=1 and

(a,n)≡a(a+1)(a+2)⋯(a+n−1)(a,n)\equiv a(a+1)(a+2)\cdots(a+n-1)

for n=1,2,3,…n=1,2,3,\ldots. For our applications to hypergeometric functions, in the sequel we will need only real parameters a,b,ca,b,c and real argument z=xz=x.

It is well known that the hypergeometric function v=F⁡(a,b,c,x)v=F(a,b;c;x) satisfies the hypergeometric differential equation

(2.2) x⁡(1−x)​v′′+[c−(a+b+1)​x]​v′−a​b​v=0.x(1-x)v^{\prime\prime}+[c-(a+b+1)x]v^{\prime}-abv=0.

We recall the derivative formula

(2.3) F′​(a,b,c,x)=dd​x​F​(a,b,c,x)=a​bc​F​(a+1,b+1,c+1,x).F^{\prime}(a,b;c;x)=\frac{d}{dx}F(a,b;c;x)=\frac{ab}{c}F(a+1,b+1;c+1;x).

The behavior of the hypergeometric function near x=1x=1 is given by

(2.4) {F(a,b;c;1)=Γ⁡(c)​Γ​(c−a−b)Γ⁡(c−a)​Γ​(c−b),c>a+b,F⁡(a,b,a+b,1−)=1B⁡(a,b)​[log⁡11−x+R⁡(a,b)]​(1+O⁡(1−x)),F(a,b;c;x)=(1−x)c−a−bF(c−a,c−b;c;x),c<a+b.\begin{cases}F(a,b;c;1)=\dfrac{\Gamma(c)\Gamma(c-a-b)}{\Gamma(c-a)\Gamma(c-b)},~c>a+b,\\ F(a,b;a+b;1-)=\dfrac{1}{B(a,b)}\Big[\log\dfrac{1}{1-x}+R(a,b)\Big](1+O(1-x)),\\ F(a,b;c;x)=(1-x)^{c-a-b}F(c-a,c-b;c;x),~c<a+b.\end{cases}

Here B⁡(a,b)B(a,b) denotes the beta function, namely,

B⁡(a,b)=Γ⁡(a)​Γ​(b)Γ⁡(a+b),B(a,b)=\frac{\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)}{\Gamma(a+b)},

and R⁡(a,b)R(a,b) is the function defined by

R⁡(a,b)=−2​γ−Ψ⁡(a)−Ψ⁡(b),R(a,b)=-2\gamma-\Psi(a)-\Psi(b),

where Ψ⁡(x)=Γ′​(x)/Γ⁡(x)\Psi(x)=\Gamma^{\prime}(x)/\Gamma(x) is the digamma function and γ\gamma is the Euler-Mascheroni constant, known to equal −Ψ⁡(1).-\Psi(1). In particular, B⁡(1/2,1/2)=πB(1/2,1/2)=\pi and R⁡(1/2,1/2)=log⁡16R(1/2,1/2)=\log 16. The asymptotic formula in (2.4) for the zero-balanced case a+b=ca+b=c is due to Ramanujan. A general formula appears in [AS, 15.3.10]. Some explicit estimates for the O⁡(1−x)O(1-x) term in the zero-balanced case are given in [AVV1, Theorem 1.52].

The following lemmas will be used in the next section.

2.5 Lemma.

For a,ba,b with a+b≠0,−1,−2,…,a+b\neq 0,-1,-2,\dots,

(1−x)​dd​x​F​(a,b,a+b,x)=a​ba+b​F​(a,b,a+b+1,x).(1-x)\frac{d}{dx}F(a,b;a+b;x)=\frac{ab}{a+b}F(a,b;a+b+1;x).
Proof.

In view of (2.3), it is enough to show the identity F⁡(a+1,b+1,a+b+1,x)=(1−x)−1​F​(a,b,a+b+1,x),F(a+1,b+1;a+b+1;x)=(1-x)^{-1}F(a,b;a+b+1;x), which follows from the third case of (2.4). ∎

A sequence {an}n=0∞\{a_{n}\}_{n=0}^{\infty} of real numbers is called totally monotone (or completely monotone) if Δk​an≥0\Delta^{k}a_{n}\geq 0 for all k,n=0,1,2,….k,n=0,1,2,\dots. Here, Δk​an\Delta^{k}a_{n} is defined inductively in kk by Δ0​an=an\Delta^{0}a_{n}=a_{n} and Δk+1​an=Δk​an−Δk​an+1.\Delta^{k+1}a_{n}=\Delta^{k}a_{n}-\Delta^{k}a_{n+1}.

2.6 Remark.

For a totally monotone sequence {an},\{a_{n}\}, Δk​an>0\Delta^{k}a_{n}>0 for k,n=0,1,2,…k,n=0,1,2,\dots unless a1=a2=a3=….a_{1}=a_{2}=a_{3}=\dots.

Indeed, Hausdorff’s theorem (cf. [Wa]) tells us that {an}\{a_{n}\} is totally monotone precisely when there exists a positive Borel measure ν\nu on I=[0,1]I=[0,1] such that

an=∫Ixn​𝑑ν​(x),(n=0,1,2,…).a_{n}=\int_{I}x^{n}d\nu(x),\quad(n=0,1,2,\dots).

Since

Δk​an=∫Ixn​(1−x)k​𝑑ν​(x),\Delta^{k}a_{n}=\int_{I}x^{n}(1-x)^{k}d\nu(x),

we have the strict inequality Δk​an>0\Delta^{k}a_{n}>0 unless ν\nu is a linear combination of the Dirac measures δ0\delta_{0} at x=0x=0 and δ1\delta_{1} at x=1.x=1. When ν=a​δ0+b​δ1\nu=a\delta_{0}+b\delta_{1} with a,b≥0,a,b\geq 0, we have a0=a+ba_{0}=a+b and a1=a2=⋯=b.a_{1}=a_{2}=\dots=b.

Küstner [K] studied hypergeometric functions from the aspect of totally monotone sequences. We need the following result for later use.

2.7 Lemma (Küstner [K, Theorem 1.5]).

Let a,b,ca,b,c be real numbers with −1≤a≤c-1\leq a\leq c and 0<b≤c.0<b\leq c. The coefficients of the power series expansion of the function F⁡(a+1,b+1,c+1,x)/F⁡(a,b,c,x)F(a+1,b+1;c+1;x)/F(a,b;c;x) about x=0x=0 form a totally monotone sequence.

Let f⁡(x)=∑n=0∞an​xnf(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}a_{n}x^{n} be a real power series convergent on (−1,1)(-1,1), and let the sequence {an}\{a_{n}\} be non-constant and monotone. Let g⁡(x)=(1−x)​f​(x)=∑n=0∞bn​xng(x)=(1-x)f(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}b_{n}x^{n}.

    If the sequence {an}\{a_{n}\} is non-increasing, then bn≤0b_{n}\leq 0, for n=1,2,…n=1,2,\ldots, with strict inequality for at least one nn. In particular, gg is strictly decreasing on [0,1)[0,1).

Clearly, b0=a0b_{0}=a_{0} and bn=an−an−1b_{n}=a_{n}-a_{n-1}, for n=1,2,3,…,n=1,2,3,\ldots, so that the assertions follow immediately. ∎

In Lemma 2.8, if the sequence {an}\{a_{n}\} is constant, then clearly g⁡(x)g(x) is constant and equals a0a_{0} for all xx.

3. Some properties of hypergeometric functions

In the present section, we investigate properties of some combinations of hypergeometric functions. Some of these will be applied to hyperbolic metric in the next section.

3.1 Lemma.

For positive numbers a,b,ca,b,c and x∈(−1,1)x\in(-1,1), we let f⁡(x)=(1−x)​F​(a,b,c,x)f(x)=(1-x)F(a,b;c;x).

  1. (1)

    If a​b≥cab\geq c, and a+b≥c+1a+b\geq c+1, with at least one of these inequalities being strict, then f′​(x)>0f^{\prime}(x)>0 on (0,1)(0,1), so that ff is strictly increasing.

  2. (2)

    If a​b≤cab\leq c, and a+b≤c+1a+b\leq c+1, with at least one of these inequalities being strict, then f′​(x)<0f^{\prime}(x)<0 on (0,1)(0,1), so that ff is strictly decreasing.

  3. (3)

    If both of the inequalities become equalities, then ff is the constant function 11.

Proof.

F⁡(a,b,c,x)=∑n=0∞Tn​xnF(a,b;c;x)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}T_{n}x^{n}, where Tn=(a,n)​(b,n)/[(c,n)​n!]T_{n}=(a,n)(b,n)/[(c,n)n!]. Hence, Tn+1/Tn=(a+n)​(b+n)/[(c+n)​(n+1)]T_{n+1}/T_{n}=(a+n)(b+n)/[(c+n)(n+1)], for n=0,1,2,…n=0,1,2,\ldots, which is non-decreasing in case (1), non-increasing in case (2), and constant in case (3). Hence the assertions follow from Lemma 2.8 and Remark 2.9. ∎

Let a,b,ca,b,c be positive numbers with max⁡{a,b}≤c\max\{a,b\}\leq c and set v⁡(x)=F⁡(a,b,c,x)v(x)=F(a,b;c;x) and

f′​(x)f⁡(x)=F′​(x)F⁡(x)−F′​(1−x)F⁡(1−x),\frac{f^{\prime}(x)}{f(x)}=\frac{F^{\prime}(x)}{F(x)}-\frac{F^{\prime}(1-x)}{F(1-x)},

  4. (4)

We put g⁡(t)=et/(1+et)g(t)=e^{t}/(1+e^{t}) and v⁡(x)=F⁡(a,b,a+b,x)v(x)=F(a,b;a+b;x) as in the proof of Theorem 3.7. We further set k⁡(x)=log⁡[v⁡(x)/v⁡(1−x)]k(x)=\log[v(x)/v(1-x)] for x∈(0,1).x\in(0,1). Then q=k∘gq=k\circ g and thus

where x=g⁡(t)x=g(t) and N⁡(x)N(x) is given in Corollary 3.4. Since N⁡(x)>0N(x)>0 by the corollary, we conclude that qq and QQ are both strictly increasing. Since f′​(t)f^{\prime}(t) is strictly increasing in 1/2<x<1,1/2<x<1, we conclude that f′​(t)<limt→+∞f′​(t)=0,f^{\prime}(t)<\lim_{t\to+\infty}f^{\prime}(t)=0, which implies that f⁡(t)f(t) is strictly decreasing.

Finally, (6) follows from (5) and the fact that f⁡(0)=1f(0)=1 and limt→+∞f⁡(t)=R⁡(a,b)/B⁡(a,b)\lim_{t\to+\infty}f(t)=R(a,b)/B(a,b) by (2.4). ∎

4. Applications to hyperbolic metric

In [SV], the function

(4.1) h⁡(t)=et​λ0,1​(−et)=π​[8​𝒦​(11+et)​𝒦​(11+e−t)]−1,t∈ℝ,h(t)=e^{t}\lambda_{0,1}(-e^{t})=\pi\left[8{\mathcal{K}}\Big(\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+e^{t}}}\Big){\mathcal{K}}\Big(\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+e^{-t}}}\Big)\right]^{-1},\ t\in\mathbb{R},

plays a special role in the estimation of the hyperbolic metric of a general plane hyperbolic domain. Let Ω\Omega be a hyperbolic domain in ℂ\mathbb{C} and set

m⁡(a,s)=infb∈∂Ω|s−log⁡|b−a||m(a,s)=\inf_{b\in\partial\Omega}\big|s-\log|b-a|\big|

for a∈∂Ωa\in\partial\Omega and s∈ℝ.s\in\mathbb{R}. Then we have, for instance,

h⁡(m⁡(a,log⁡|z−a|))≤|z−a|​ρΩ​(z)≤π4​m​(a,log⁡|z−a|),z∈Ω,h(m(a,\log|z-a|))\leq|z-a|\rho_{\Omega}(z)\leq\frac{\pi}{4m(a,\log|z-a|)},\quad z\in\Omega,

for every a∈∂Ω.a\in\partial\Omega. By the inequality h⁡(t)≥1/(2​|t|+2​C0),h(t)\geq 1/(2|t|+2C_{0}), which is essentially due to J. Hempel, we can reproduce the sharp version of the Beardon-Pommerenke inequality (see [SV] for details). Here,

(4.2) C0=12​λ0,1​(−1)=4π​𝒦​(1/2)2=Γ​(1/4)44​π2≈4.37688.C_{0}=\frac{1}{2\lambda_{0,1}(-1)}=\frac{4}{\pi}{\mathcal{K}}(1/\sqrt{2})^{2}=\frac{\Gamma(1/4)^{4}}{4\pi^{2}}\approx 4.37688.

In the course of their investigation, the second and fourth authors arrived at some conjectures (Conjecture 2.12 in [SV]), which we are now able to prove. We remark that there is a slight error in the statement of Conjecture 2.12(3) of [SV]: the interval (−π/4,π/4)(-\pi/4,\pi/4) has to be replaced by (−2,2)(-2,2) as in (3) below.

  1. (1)

Theorem 4.3 has an application to the hyperbolic metric. For a hyperbolic domain Ω\Omega in ℂ,\mathbb{C}, we consider the quantity

σΩ​(z)=supa,b∈∂Ωλa,b​(z),z∈Ω.\sigma_{\Omega}(z)=\sup_{a,b\in\partial\Omega}\lambda_{a,b}(z),\quad z\in\Omega.

Thus, σΩ​(z)≤ρΩ​(z).\sigma_{\Omega}(z)\leq\rho_{\Omega}(z). Gardiner and Lakic [GL] proved that ρΩ​(z)≤A​σΩ​(z)\rho_{\Omega}(z)\leq A\sigma_{\Omega}(z) for an absolute constant A.A. We denote by A0A_{0} the smallest possible constant A.A. In [SV] it is shown that A0≤2​C0+π/2≈10.3246A_{0}\leq 2C_{0}+\pi/2\approx 10.3246 and observed (see Remark 3.2 in [SV]) that this could be improved to A0≤1/h⁡(π/4)=H⁡(π/4)≈9.0157A_{0}\leq 1/h(\pi/4)=H(\pi/4)\approx 9.0157 if assertion (1) in Theorem 4.3 were true. In [SV], the function φ⁡(t)=2​Φ​(et/2)\varphi(t)=2\Phi(e^{t/2}) plays an important role in the estimation of the hyperbolic distance, where Φ⁡(x)\Phi(x) is as in (1.1). In view of (1.1) and (1.2), we have the expression

φ⁡(t)=log⁡F⁡(12,12,1,et/21+et/2)F⁡(12,12,1,11+et/2)=q⁡(t/2),\varphi(t)=\log\frac{F\big(\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{1}{2};1;\frac{e^{t/2}}{1+e^{t/2}}\big)}{F\big(\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{1}{2};1;\frac{1}{1+e^{t/2}}\big)}=q(t/2),

where qq is the function defined in Theorem 3.8 with a=b=1/2.a=b=1/2. Thus, as a corollary of Theorem 3.8, we obtain the following.

4.5 Corollary.

The function φ⁡(t)/t\varphi(t)/t is strictly decreasing on (0,∞)(0,\infty), implying that φ⁡(t)\varphi(t) is subadditive on (0,∞)(0,\infty).

The statement of Corollary 4.5 was given as Conjecture 5.9 in [SV]. This conjecture has recently been settled by Baricz [Ba] by a different method.

As an application of Corollary 4.5, we give an improvement of Theorem 5.12 in [SV].

4.6 Theorem.

Let a0,a1,a2,…a_{0},a_{1},a_{2},\dots be an infinite sequence of distinct complex numbers with the properties

  1. (1)

    0=|a0|<|a1|≤|a2|≤…,0=|a_{0}|<|a_{1}|\leq|a_{2}|\leq\dots,

  2. (2)

    |an+1|≤ec​|an||a_{n+1}|\leq e^{c}|a_{n}| for n=1,2,3,…,n=1,2,3,\dots, where c>0c>0 is a constant, and

  3. (3)

    |an|→∞|a_{n}|\to\infty as n→∞.n\to\infty.

If a domain Ω\Omega in ℂ\mathbb{C} omits all the points an,a_{n}, then

(4.7) dΩ​(z1,z2)≥A⁡(log⁡|z2|−log⁡|z1|)−Bd_{\Omega}(z_{1},z_{2})\geq A\big(\log|z_{2}|-\log|z_{1}|\big)-B

for z1,z2∈Ωz_{1},z_{2}\in\Omega with e−c/2|a1|≤|z1|≤|z2|.e^{-c/2}|a_{1}|\leq|z_{1}|\leq|z_{2}|. Here, A=φ⁡(c)/cA=\varphi(c)/c and B=φ⁡(c)−φ⁡(c/2).B=\varphi(c)-\varphi(c/2).

Proof.

We use the same argument indicated in [SV, p. 901].

Choose integers kk and ll with 1≤k≤l1\leq k\leq l, so that |ak​ak−1|≤|z1|≤|ak​ak+1|\sqrt{|a_{k}a_{k-1}|}\leq|z_{1}|\leq\sqrt{|a_{k}a_{k+1}|} and |al​al−1|≤|z2|≤|al​al+1|\sqrt{|a_{l}a_{l-1}|}\leq|z_{2}|\leq\sqrt{|a_{l}a_{l+1}|} hold. Then, Theorem 1.7 in [SV] gives us

dΩ​(z1,z2)≥12​φ​(tk−log⁡|z1|)+∑n=k+1lφ⁡(tn−tn−1)+12​φ​(log⁡|z2|−tl),d_{\Omega}(z_{1},z_{2})\geq\frac{1}{2}\varphi(t_{k}-\log|z_{1}|)+\sum_{n=k+1}^{l}\varphi(t_{n}-t_{n-1})+\frac{1}{2}\varphi(\log|z_{2}|-t_{l}),

where tn=log⁡|an|.t_{n}=\log|a_{n}|. Noting that tn−tn−1≤c,tk−log⁡|z1|≤c/2t_{n}-t_{n-1}\leq c,~t_{k}-\log|z_{1}|\leq c/2 and log⁡|z2|−tl≤c/2,\log|z_{2}|-t_{l}\leq c/2, we deduce from the monotonicity of φ⁡(t)/t\varphi(t)/t the chain of inequalities

dΩ​(z1,z2)\displaystyle\quad d_{\Omega}(z_{1},z_{2})
≥12​(tk−log⁡|z1|)​φ⁡(c/2)c/2+∑n=k+1l(tn−tn−1)​φ⁡(c)c+12​(log⁡|z2|−tl)​φ⁡(c/2)c/2\displaystyle\geq\frac{1}{2}(t_{k}-\log|z_{1}|)\frac{\varphi(c/2)}{c/2}+\sum_{n=k+1}^{l}(t_{n}-t_{n-1})\frac{\varphi(c)}{c}+\frac{1}{2}(\log|z_{2}|-t_{l})\frac{\varphi(c/2)}{c/2}
=φ⁡(c)c​(log⁡|z2|−log⁡|z1|)−φ⁡(c)−φ⁡(c/2)c​(tk−log⁡|z1|+log⁡|z2|−tl)\displaystyle=\frac{\varphi(c)}{c}(\log|z_{2}|-\log|z_{1}|)-\frac{\varphi(c)-\varphi(c/2)}{c}(t_{k}-\log|z_{1}|+\log|z_{2}|-t_{l})
≥φ⁡(c)c​(log⁡|z2|−log⁡|z1|)+φ⁡(c)−φ⁡(c/2).\displaystyle\geq\frac{\varphi(c)}{c}(\log|z_{2}|-\log|z_{1}|)+\varphi(c)-\varphi(c/2).

∎

Under the same hypothesis as in Theorem 4.6, Theorem 5.12 in [SV] asserts (4.7) with A=h⁡(c/2)A=h(c/2) and B=0,B=0, where hh is given by (4.1). Also, (5.17) of [SV] gives (4.7) with A=(1/c)​log⁡(1+c/(2​C0))A=(1/c)\log(1+c/(2C_{0})) and B=c/(4​π).B=c/(4\pi). Compare the graphs of the functions φ⁡(c)/c,h⁡(c/2)\varphi(c)/c,h(c/2) and (1/c)​log⁡(1+c/(2​C0))(1/c)\log(1+c/(2C_{0})) (Figure 1).
